sections.h: Antioch: the first church of Jews and Gentiles
sections.b: After Peter's defense in Jerusalem (Acts 11:1–18), the church accepts that God has "given even the Gentiles repentance that brings life." At Antioch in Syria unnamed believers from Cyprus and Cyrene begin telling Gentiles about the Lord Jesus, and the first mixed church of Jews and Gentiles grows up, where the disciples are first called "Christians" (Acts 11:19–26). Its leaders include a Cypriot Levite, an African, a man raised at Herod's court and Saul of Tarsus (Acts 13:1).

sections.h: God-fearers and proselytes in the synagogues
sections.b: Paul's sermon at Pisidian Antioch addresses both "Israelites" and "you who fear God" (Acts 13:16, 26): Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God and attended the synagogue without being circumcised. Proselytes, full converts, also follow Paul (Acts 13:43). Inscriptions such as the donor list from Aphrodisias, which lists Jews, proselytes and "God-fearers" separately, confirm that such sympathizers existed. They were often the first to believe, and through them Paul's mission moved from the synagogue to the city.
sections.refs: Acts 13:16; Acts 13:26; Acts 13:43; Acts 13:48; Acts 13:50; Acts 10:2

sections.h: "A door of faith" for the Gentiles
sections.b: Paul and Barnabas end their first journey by reporting that God "had opened to the Gentiles a door to faith" (Acts 14:27). The phrase sums up the first mission: Gentiles enter God's people by believing, without first becoming Jews. Whether they must also be circumcised and keep the Law is the question the council in Jerusalem takes up next (Acts 15).

common: The church at Antioch was the first congregation in which many Gentiles believed alongside Jews.
uncommon: A few scholars, following A. T. Kraabel, doubted that a recognized class of Gentile "God-fearers" existed outside Luke's story; most now think the Aphrodisias inscription answers the doubt.

sections.h: Peter's defense: the sheet and the table (Acts 11)
sections.b: Peter is criticized in Jerusalem not for preaching to Gentiles but for eating with them (Acts 11:3). He answers by retelling his vision of a sheet full of every kind of animal and the command "Get up, Peter; kill and eat," with God's reply, "What God has made clean, you must not call common" (Acts 11:5–10). Peter applies it to people (Acts 10:28); whether it also abolishes the food laws is read differently by most churches, by Messianic Jews and by Seventh-day Adventists.

Peter refuses anything "common or unclean" (Acts 11:8). The two words may differ: akathartos is the unclean animal of Leviticus 11; koinos, "common," may mean clean food defiled by contact. God answers with the first word: "you must not call common."

Peter's defense rests on the Spirit: "the Holy Spirit fell on them, the same way he fell on us in the beginning" (Acts 11:15), and God gave them "the same gift" (Acts 11:17). He recalls Jesus' promise, "John baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit" (Acts 11:16; Acts 1:5). In Antioch the Spirit speaks to the praying church and sends out Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:2–4), fills Paul to confront a magician (Acts 13:9), and fills the new disciples with joy even after their teachers are driven out (Acts 13:52).

Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, ruled all Judea as king from AD 41 to 44. He executed James son of Zebedee and imprisoned Peter to please the people of Jerusalem (Acts 12:1–4). At Caesarea, hailed as a god, he was struck down and died (Acts 12:20–23). Josephus tells the same death: a silver robe shining in the theater, flatterers calling him a god, and five days of pain (Jewish Antiquities 19.343–350). His son Agrippa II hears Paul in Acts 25–26.

Peter explains to the Jerusalem believers why he ate with Gentiles, telling his vision and the gift of the Spirit "in order" (Acts 11:4–17). Arrested by Agrippa at Passover, he is freed by an angel in a story told with echoes of the Exodus and of Jesus' passion (Acts 12:3–17). He sends word to James and leaves "for somewhere else" (Acts 12:17); Catholic tradition placed his arrival in Rome about this time, though most historians date his Roman ministry later.

James son of Zebedee, one of the three closest to Jesus, was executed with the sword by Herod Agrippa about AD 44 (Acts 12:2), fulfilling Jesus' word that he would drink his cup (Matthew 20:23). Unlike Judas, he is not replaced: a faithful apostle who dies keeps his place among the Twelve.

sections.h: An angel at the prison, an angel at the throne
sections.b: In Acts 12 an angel of the Lord frees Peter from prison and later strikes Herod down; the same verb, "strike," is used of both (Acts 12:7, 23). The believers in Mary's house think Peter's knock must be "his angel" (Acts 12:15), evidence of the belief that God assigns angels to watch over people (Matthew 18:10; Genesis 48:16).

After Paul turns to the Gentiles at Pisidian Antioch, "as many as had been assigned to eternal life came to believe" (Acts 13:48). The perfect participle tetagmenoi ("assigned, appointed") is read by Reformed interpreters as God's eternal election causing faith, and by Arminian and Wesleyan interpreters as those who were then disposed or ready to believe. Luke sets it against those whom Paul describes as "judging yourselves unworthy of eternal life" (Acts 13:46), holding God's appointing and human response together.

sections.h: Elders in the churches of Acts
sections.b: Besides the twenty-four elders of Revelation, the New Testament names elders as leaders of local churches. They appear first in Jerusalem, receiving the famine relief from Antioch (Acts 11:30), and later stand beside the apostles at the council (Acts 15:2–6, 22–23) and with James (Acts 21:18). On their first journey Paul and Barnabas "chose elders" in each new church with prayer and fasting (Acts 14:23); the verb, cheirotoneō, once meant "elect by show of hands" and later became the Greek word for ordination. The model was the elders of Jewish towns and synagogues. Later letters treat elders and overseers as one office (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7), and how this grew into the bishops, presbyters and deacons of later centuries is debated among the churches.
sections.refs: Acts 11:30; Acts 14:23; Acts 15:2–6; Acts 20:17; Acts 20:28; Acts 21:18; Titus 1:5–7; 1 Timothy 5:17; James 5:14

common: Most churches trace their ordained ministry, in one form or another, to the elders the apostles appointed in Acts.
uncommon: Some argue from the old sense of cheirotoneō in Acts 14:23 that the congregations themselves elected their elders by vote.

sections.h: Justification in Paul's sermon at Pisidian Antioch
sections.b: The only use of "justify" in Paul's speeches in Acts: "There were things from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses. From all of them, everyone who believes is justified in him" (Acts 13:39). Most read it as Paul's teaching in the letters (Romans 3:20–28; Galatians 2:16): the law could acquit no one, faith in Christ acquits from everything. Philipp Vielhauer read it as "partial" justification by the law completed by faith and argued that Luke misunderstood Paul.

sections.h: David's promise in Paul's first sermon
sections.b: Paul tells Israel's story up to David, "a man to suit my heart" (Acts 13:22), and announces that "out of this man's offspring, as he had promised, God has brought Israel a Savior, Jesus" (Acts 13:23). The promise of 2 Samuel 7:12–16 is kept in the resurrection: Isaiah 55:3's "holy things of David, the ones that are sure" belong to the Holy One who did not see decay (Acts 13:34–37).

sections.h: "This day I have fathered you" and the resurrection
sections.b: Paul applies Psalm 2:7, the coronation word to David's heir, to God's raising of Jesus (Acts 13:33), as Romans 1:4 and Hebrews 1:5 also do. Some read this as an early belief that Jesus became God's Son at the resurrection; others note that Luke calls him God's Son from his conception (Luke 1:35), so the resurrection enthrones a sonship that was already his.
sections.refs: Acts 13:33; Psalm 2:7; Romans 1:3–4; Hebrews 1:5; Luke 1:35; Luke 3:22

sections.b: Paul and Barnabas quote the Greek of Isaiah 49:6, "I have set you as a light for the nations," as the Lord's command to them (Acts 13:47). Simeon had applied the same words to the infant Jesus (Luke 2:32), and Paul uses the picture again of his own calling (Acts 26:17–18, 23). In Acts the Servant's mission to the nations continues through Jesus' messengers.

At Pisidian Antioch Paul says God's word "had to be told to you first," but since some reject it, "we are turning to the Gentiles" (Acts 13:46). He says it again at Corinth (Acts 18:6) and Rome (Acts 28:28), yet in the next city he goes to the synagogue (Acts 14:1). Jacob Jervell read Acts as showing Israel divided, with many Jews believing; Jack T. Sanders read it as hostile to Jews; Joseph Tyson traced a movement from hope to rejection.
sections.refs: Acts 13:5; Acts 13:46; Acts 14:1; Acts 18:6; Acts 28:25–28; Romans 1:16; Romans 11:1–2

sections.b: At Lystra, after a healing, the crowd hails Barnabas as Zeus and Paul as Hermes, and the priest of Zeus brings bulls to sacrifice (Acts 14:11–13). The apostles tear their clothes and call the people from "these empty things," the Greek Old Testament's word for idols, to "the God who lives, who made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them" (Acts 14:15). Ovid's tale of Zeus and Hermes visiting Phrygia in disguise helps explain the crowd's reaction.

On Cyprus a Jewish magician and false prophet, Bar-Jesus, also called Elymas, served in the circle of the proconsul Sergius Paulus and tried to turn him from the faith. Paul calls him "son of the devil" and strikes him blind for a time, and the proconsul believes (Acts 13:6–12). Josephus tells of another Cypriot Jewish magician at the court of the governor Felix (Jewish Antiquities 20.142). The scene parallels Peter's confrontation with Simon the magician (Acts 8:9–24).

sections.h: A king hailed as a god (Acts 12:22)
sections.b: At Caesarea the crowd cries that Herod Agrippa's voice is "a god speaking, not a man," and he is struck down "because he did not give the glory to God" (Acts 12:22–23); Josephus agrees that he failed to reject the flattery. In contrast Peter refuses Cornelius' worship (Acts 10:25–26) and Paul and Barnabas refuse sacrifice at Lystra (Acts 14:14–15).

Christian prophets travel from Jerusalem to Antioch, and one, Agabus, foretells a great famine, which leads the church to send relief to Judea (Acts 11:27–30). The leaders of the Antioch church are "prophets and teachers" (Acts 13:1), and the Spirit's command to set apart Barnabas and Saul probably came through one of them (Acts 13:2).

Warned of famine, the disciples at Antioch each give "as far as his means allowed" and send aid to the believers in Judea by Barnabas and Saul (Acts 11:29–30). It is the first gift from one church to another, the pattern for Paul's later collection for Jerusalem's poor (1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8–9; Romans 15:25–27). The famine is attested by Josephus for Judea about AD 46–48 (Jewish Antiquities 20.51–53).

sections.h: The Creator's witness in rain and harvest (Acts 14:15–17)
sections.b: To people who knew nothing of Israel's Scriptures, Paul and Barnabas proclaim the God "who made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them," who "did not leave himself without a witness," giving rain, fruitful seasons, food and good cheer (Acts 14:15–17). The same appeal to creation shapes Paul's speech at Athens (Acts 17:24–28) and Romans 1:19–20, and underlies Christian teaching on general revelation.

sections.h: Signs and wonders on the first journey
sections.b: On Paul's first journey the Lord "backed up the word of his grace" with signs and wonders (Acts 14:3). Paul blinds the magician Elymas (Acts 13:11) and heals a man lame from birth at Lystra, a healing that closely matches Peter's at the temple gate (Acts 14:8–10; Acts 3:1–10). Paul's own letters speak of the signs of an apostle and of miracles among the Galatians (2 Corinthians 12:12; Galatians 3:5).
sections.refs: Acts 13:11; Acts 14:3; Acts 14:8–10; Acts 3:1–10; Romans 15:19; Galatians 3:5

sections.b: Acts reserves "apostle" for the Twelve, except in Acts 14:4 and 14:14, where Barnabas and Paul are "the apostles." The word may mean envoys sent by the church at Antioch (Acts 13:3), as in 2 Corinthians 8:23, or it may reflect the claim Paul makes in his letters to be an apostle called by the risen Christ (Galatians 1:1).
sections.refs: Acts 14:4; Acts 14:14; Acts 1:21–26; Acts 13:1–3; Galatians 1:1; 1 Corinthians 9:1–6

sections.b: Barnabas brings Saul from Tarsus to teach at Antioch (Acts 11:25–26), and they take famine relief to Jerusalem (Acts 11:30; 12:25), a visit some identify with Galatians 2:1–10. Sent out by the Spirit (Acts 13:2–4), Saul "who also went by Paul" takes the lead from Cyprus on (Acts 13:9, 13). His sermon at Pisidian Antioch is his longest to Jews in Acts (Acts 13:16–41). At Lystra he is first hailed as a god, then stoned and left for dead (Acts 14:11–19; 2 Corinthians 11:25). The journey, about AD 46–48, founded the churches of south Galatia.
sections.refs: Acts 11:25–30; Acts 12:25; Acts 13:1–14:28; Galatians 1:21–2:10; 2 Corinthians 11:25; 2 Timothy 3:11

sections.b: Returning to the cities where they had been attacked, Paul and Barnabas strengthen the new disciples and tell them, "We must go through many troubles to enter the kingdom of God" (Acts 14:22). Paul had just been stoned at Lystra (Acts 14:19). The teaching matches Paul's letters (1 Thessalonians 3:3–4; 2 Timothy 3:11–12).

sections.h: Psalm 16 and David's tomb in Paul's sermon
sections.b: Like Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:25–32), Paul argues from Psalm 16:10 in its Greek form: "You will not allow your holy one to see decay." David served his generation, died and decayed, but the one God raised did not (Acts 13:34–37). The Greek Old Testament's "decay" for the Hebrew "Pit" suits the argument.

Acts marks the stages of its story with summaries in which the word of God grows like a living thing (Acts 6:7; 12:24; 19:20). In chapter 12 the summary follows the death of the king who attacked the church: "But the word of God kept growing and multiplying" (Acts 12:24), echoing Israel's growth under Pharaoh (Exodus 1:7).
